name: Pattern 1: Draft, Then a Person Edits
title: Pattern 1: Draft, Then a Person Edits
answer: Draft, Then a Person Edits is the most common pattern in this volume: an AI tool produces a first version of a document and a person reads it, corrects it, and decides whether it is released. It matters because the draft is only a starting point, and the person who signs the work owns it, so the quality of the final product depends on real human editing rather than a quick glance.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: This pattern describes AI as a fast assistant rather than an author. A tool writes a first version of a lesson plan, a parent letter, practice questions, a rubric, a summary of an individualized education program for a parent, or a grant narrative, and a person then reads it, fixes it, and decides whether it goes out. It solves the problem of the blank page by giving the adult something to react to, while keeping judgment and ownership with the person who signs the document. The pattern is simple to state, but it only works when the editing is genuine and the adult stays responsible for what is released.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a preschool classroom, a teacher might ask an approved tool to draft the weekly note home and then add the class news that only she knows. In a middle school, a science teacher might request three versions of the same reading at different levels and then check that the science stayed correct in all three. In a high school, a counselor might draft a plain language explanation of graduation requirements for families. Across all these cases the tool saves the blank page and the adult supplies the judgment. Figure 2.3 sets out four steps that make the pattern safe, and the checking becomes stricter as the stakes rise.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with practice-based evidence drawn from studies it cites. In one study, 15 teachers in five English primary schools used AI for lesson planning over two terms and reported that their weekly planning time fell from about 10 hours to under 5 (Carson et al., 2026). The same teachers said the saved time was often swallowed by other demands, so the hours never turned into anything a principal could see. In another study, when researchers asked a chatbot to write a first grade science lesson, the result was well organized and followed a familiar teaching model, but it included questionable steps, left out details, and listed a teaching resource that did not exist (Powell & Courchesne, 2024). A teacher who skimmed it would have handed a fake source to a room full of six year olds, which shows the draft was useful only because a careful adult was going to read every line.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits of this pattern are that drafts need real editing rather than a quick glance, and that time savings can disappear into other demands. For anything touching a student's services, grades, or records, the names come out before the text goes in, and the final version is checked against the real file. That rule is easy to state and easy to skip, which is why it appears in every chapter that uses this pattern. The decisions that stay with a person are whether the draft is accurate, whether it is appropriate, and whether it goes out at all. The person who signs the document owns it, and the AI remains closer to a fast assistant than an author.
